extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, in-house counsel and rights holders involved in Brazilian patent enforcement and litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for seeking and defending patent-related remedies (confidentiality, ADR, injunctions, damages, search/seizure, enforcement, and appeals) under Brazilian law (CPC and LPI). Useful for practitioners conducting or advising on patent enforcement actions in Brazil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality — closed proceedings under Article 189 CPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural acts are public, but certain cases are processed closed to the public per Article 189 CPC: I) when public or social interest requires; II) family law matters; III) cases containing data protected by the constitutional right to privacy; IV) arbitration-related cases where confidentiality is evidenced before the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A request to close proceedings must be accompanied by grounds; the judge decides and that decision is interlocutory (appealable). Paragraphs restrict access to case records for closed proceedings to parties and their attorneys; third parties who demonstrate legal interest may request limited certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of confidential information in court — Article 206 LPI
rubrics_metrics.description: If confidential information (industrial or commercial secrets) is disclosed in court for defense of a party’s interests, the judge must determine that the case proceed closed to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge also must prohibit the use of such information by the other party for other purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and seizure in patent process-crimes — expert accompaniment
rubrics_metrics.description: During search and seizure in a crime against a process patent the court officer will be accompanied by an expert who preliminarily verifies the existence of the illicit act; the judge may order seizure of products obtained by the infringing party by means of the patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure is also available in civil actions; the expert’s preliminary verification is a procedural requirement in these seizures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of alternative dispute resolution (conciliation/mediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary procedure provides for a conciliation or mediation hearing soon after filing (Article 334 CPC), and judges may adopt alternative conciliation methods at any time (Article 3 CPC); parties may hold conciliation pre-procedure and an agreement approved by a judge is enforceable in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADR can be used before or during litigation; court-approved agreements have enforceability as instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation regime and mediator qualifications (Law No. 13,140/15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation is a technical activity by an impartial third party without decision-making power who assists parties to develop mutually agreed solutions; mediators must meet minimum education and training requirements and be registered with courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediator must have a higher education degree obtained at least two years prior and training from recognized mediation institutions; courts maintain registers and set compensation borne by the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of mediation (Law No. 13,140/15, Article 14 and 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: All information relating to mediation is confidential with respect to third parties and may not be disclosed in arbitration or court proceedings unless parties decide otherwise or disclosure is required by law or to comply with the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty of confidentiality applies to mediator, parties, representatives, lawyers, technical advisors and others involved. Confidential items include statements, recognitions of fact, acceptances of proposals, and documents prepared solely for mediation. Evidence violating these provisions will not be admitted in arbitral or judicial proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctive relief standard — likelihood of right and danger of damage (Article 300 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocutory (injunctive) relief is granted when there is evidence of the likelihood of the right and danger of damage or risk to the useful outcome of the case (Article 300 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge may require security interest or personal guarantee to compensate the other party for damage; the requirement may be waived for economically disadvantaged parties. Relief may be provisional or anticipatory; anticipatory relief that seeks to anticipate the final claim may only be granted when its effects are reversible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of interlocutory relief (Article 301 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocutory relief intended to ensure the useful outcome can be effected by attachment, sequestration, listing of property, registration of protest against disposition of property, or any other suitable measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge selects measures suitable to ensure the right; the relief is aimed at preserving the effectiveness of the eventual judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for damages caused by interlocutory relief (Article 302 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party is liable for damage caused by the effectiveness of interlocutory relief if: I) the judgment is unfavorable to them; II) the party fails to provide means for service within five days after obtaining advance interlocutory relief; III) the effectiveness of the measure is ceased; or IV) the judge accepts preemption or limitation of plaintiff’s claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability applies regardless of redress for procedural damage; security or guarantee requirements exist to mitigate this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory relief requested in advance — procedural requirements (Article 303–304 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory relief may be requested in advance and the complaint may be limited to the request for relief and indication of the final request. If such relief is granted, the plaintiff must amend the complaint within 15 days (or longer set by judge) or face termination of the case without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If granted and not appealed, the interlocutory relief requested in advance becomes final and the case may be terminated; parties have procedural obligations (service to defendant, possible conciliation hearing). There is a two-year limit to review/change/ invalidate an interlocutory relief requested in advance that was not questioned and filed (Article 304(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional injunction requested in advance — procedural timeline (Articles 305–308 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional injunction requested in advance must indicate the dispute, grounds, right being pursued, and possible damage; defendant is served and given five days to answer and indicate evidence; if no answer, plaintiff’s facts are deemed accepted and judge decides on provisional injunction within five days. After provisional injunction is effected, plaintiff must make main request within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff fails to make main request within the term, or injunction not effected within 30 days, or judge dismisses main request, the provisional injunction ceases to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory relief based on evidence (Article 311 CPC) — grounds that dispense danger-of-damage requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief under Article 311 is granted regardless of the demonstration of danger of damage when: I) there is abuse of right of defense or obvious dilatory intentions; II) allegations can be evidenced only through documents and a theory is confirmed in repeated cases or binding precedent; III) repossession claim based on adequate documentary evidence; or IV) complaint is accompanied by sufficient documentary evidence to which defendant presents no opposing evidence capable of generating reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In items II and III the judge may decide in advance; these provisions permit relief based primarily on documentary evidence or demonstrable abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of expert evidence where risk of irreversible damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Because interlocutory relief requires plausibility of alleged facts, the judge may anticipate the production of expert evidence if granting the request may result in risk of irreversible damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a discretionary procedural tool to secure evidence before relief is implemented when irreparable harm is feared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to damages for patent infringement — scope and pre-grant exploitation (Article 44 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder has right to compensation for improper exploitation of the patent subject matter, including exploitation occurring between publication of the application and grant. If infringer had knowledge of application content prior to publication, compensation period counts from date exploitation began. For biological material deposits, compensation only when material accessible to public. Right limited to patent subject matter per Article 41.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages are determined by benefits the injured party would have received; statute of limitation for damages action is five years (Article 225 LPI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of recoverable damages — compensatory scope (Articles 208–209 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Full compensation is possible for property damage and loss of profits; LPI also allows actions for damages from acts of unfair competition and civil legislation rights (including possibly pain and suffering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazilian jurists/case law recognize compensation for pain and suffering (in re ipsa) reflecting punitive and compensatory functions. Damages include emergent damage and loss of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of profits calculation criteria (Article 210 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of profits is determined by whichever is most favorable to injured party: I) benefits the injured party would have received had violation not taken place; II) benefits that the infringing party received; or III) compensation the infringing party would have paid under a legal license. Choice depends on difficulty of proof and factual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 208 and 210 must be read jointly; the winning patent holder chooses the criterion most favorable and practicable given evidence. Damages can be set in settlement or indicated in complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorneys’ fees in civil actions (Article 85 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing party pays loss-of-suit fees and procedural expenses, including experts’ fees and opposing party’s attorneys’ fees. Article 85 CPC sets attorneys’ fees at 10–20% of decision amount, economic benefit obtained, or adjusted amount where measure cannot be quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge considers professional’s degree of diligence, place of service, nature and importance of the case, and work performed when fixing the percentage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and seizure provisional measures (Articles 201–204 LPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles 201–204 LPI specify provisional search and seizure measures that may be requested; for crimes against invention-process patents the court officer is accompanied by an expert who preliminarily verifies illicit acts and judge may order seizure of products obtained by infringing process. Bad-faith requesters liable for damages (Article 204).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When industrial/commercial establishments are lawfully organized and publicly functioning, preliminary procedures are limited to inspection and seizure of products; lawful activities cannot be interrupted (Article 203).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of judgments — provisional and final compliance (CPC Articles 513–538)
rubrics_metrics.description: No specific LPI enforcement provisions; general CPC rules apply. Provisional compliance (Articles 513–522) may be ordered in urgent situations; final compliance (Articles 523–538) applies after final unappealable decision. Appeals may have effect of supersedeas suspending decision effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices of compliance and methods of enforcement are specifically regulated (e.g., notification methods, instruments enforceable under Article 515).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional compliance particularities (Article 520–521 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional compliance subject to particularities: I) creditor must repair damage if decision changed; II) becomes ineffective if later modified/annulled; III) partial modification leads to partial ineffectiveness; IV) withdrawal of cash deposits and transfer acts subject to bond arbitrated by judge. The bond may be waived in specific circumstances (support credit, creditor need, pending interlocutory appeal under Article 1042, or alignment with higher-court precedent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sole Paragraph: bond requirement maintained when dismissal may result in manifest risk of serious damage of difficult or uncertain redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to enforcement and stays (Article 525 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment debtor may file an objection during enforcement and may request stay of execution if the execution would cause serious damage difficult to redress, provided court is secured by sufficient levy, bond, or deposit. An objection does not prevent execution acts unless stay is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stay (effects of supersedeas) concerns only part of the execution, enforcement continues for the remaining part. Effects on co-debtors: granting supersedeas to one objecting debtor does not suspend enforcement against those who did not object if grounds exclusively concern the objecting party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debtor’s pre-notification offer and calculation (Article 526 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before notification to comply, defendant may appear and offer payment of amount they consider due with detailed calculation; plaintiff may object to the deposit while withdrawing undisputed amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no objection to deposit, judge declares obligation satisfied and extinguishes the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement measures for obligations to do or not to do (Articles 536–537 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: To enforce obligations to do or not do, judge may order measures including fines, search and seizure, removal of people and things, destruction of works, prevention of harmful activities and request police assistance. Fines do not depend on party request and may be applied in various phases; judge may modify amount or periodicity of the fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fine must be sufficient and compatible with the obligation and a reasonable term for compliance must be established; amounts due to the judgment creditor; provisional enforcement of fine possible if deposited in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search warrant/vesting of possession for noncompliance (Article 538 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to deliver something within the term established in the decision, a search warrant or vesting of possession may be issued in favor of the creditor, depending on whether the property is movable or real estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete enforcement remedy for delivery obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of judge’s cognizance and preclusion (pleading phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge’s cognizance on matters of fact and law is defined during the pleading phase; parties have the burden to discharge procedural burden by clearly indicating theories and evidence under penalty of procedural preclusion. If plaintiff fails to make claim adequately, judge’s cognizance limited to what was requested (Article 141 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-trial order defines disputed points and binds the judgment. Failure to present facts/arguments in pleading phase may preclude later raising of those matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final judgment (resolution on the merits) — Article 487 CPC
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Article 487 CPC there is resolution on the merits if the judge: I) accepts or rejects the request in action or counterclaim; II) decides on preemption or limitation at judge’s initiative or request; or III) approves acknowledgement of merits, transaction, or waiver. Other situations (Article 485) can terminate the case without consideration of merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding what constitutes a merits decision is essential for appealability and further procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions for clarification — purpose and term (Articles 1,022–1,027; Article 219 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for clarification aim to clarify a decision or remedy omission/contradiction and are directed to the court that rendered the decision; they are not principally intended to modify the decision. Term for motions for clarification is five days (Article 219 CPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on the remedy, a motion for clarification may sometimes produce a change in understanding and thus affect appeal timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals types, admissibility and time limits (Article 994, Article 1,003 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 994 lists permitted appeals under Brazilian law (appeal from final judgment, interlocutory appeal, internal interlocutory appeal, motion for clarification, ordinary appeal, appeals to STJ/STF, interlocutory appeal from appeals to STJ/STF, appeal against divergent decision). Term for appeals generally 15 days from publication; appeals do not prevent effectiveness of decision unless law or court decision provides otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different appeals have distinct admissibility rules and effects; parties must track specific procedural prerequisites such as prior motions for clarification where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may appeal and cross-appeals (Articles 996–998 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals may be filed by the losing party, an aggrieved third party, or the Public Prosecutor’s Office. Cross-appeals by a defeated co-party are possible in appeals from final judgment and higher-court appeals but are subordinate to the main appeal and not heard if the main appeal is withdrawn or inadmissible. An appellant may withdraw the appeal at any time without respondent consent, except in matters of general repercussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party appellants must demonstrate that the decision may affect their claimed right; withdrawal restrictions apply where general repercussion is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal bond payment requirement and exemptions (Article 1,007 CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing an appeal, the appellant must evidence payment of the appeal bond including remittance and return fees under penalty of dismissal. Appeals by certain public entities and exempt parties are exempt from payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemptions include Public Prosecutor’s Office, federal/state/municipal governments and their autonomous agencies, and those enjoying legal exemption.
